title: SDS vs Product Label: Key Differences
excerpt: An SDS is a detailed workplace hazard-information document, while a product label communicates information on or with the product and may carry legally enforceable directions for regulated products.
content_html:
An SDS and a product label both communicate important information, but they serve different roles. The SDS is a structured workplace hazard-information document; the label is the information presented on or with the actual product.

SDS: detailed hazard reference

The SDS uses a standardized 16-section format to organize product identity, hazards, composition, controls, physical properties and other safety information.

Label: information attached to the product

The label identifies the product and communicates key hazard, precautionary and use information directly where the product is handled.

Some labels carry legal use requirements

For EPA-registered pesticide products, the label is legally enforceable and defines approved directions, precautions and conditions of use. An SDS does not replace those label requirements.

The documents work together

In a workplace, the label supports immediate identification and communication at the container, while the SDS provides a fuller hazard-information reference for the exact product.

Use matching, current documents

The SDS and label should correspond to the actual product in use. A document for a similar chemical or another formulation should not be treated as interchangeable.

Practical takeaway

The label tells you about the product at the point of use; the SDS provides the structured workplace hazard reference. Neither should be casually substituted for the other.

References

  1. OSHA — Hazard Communication Questions and Answers.
  2. US EPA — Introduction to Pesticide Labels.
